threats.title: The same authorization is settled twice
threats.threat: A seller, a buyer or anyone holding a payment sends the same PAYMENT-SIGNATURE to /settle again, one after another or many at once, hoping the payer is charged more than once.
threats.stellar: An exact or upto authorization is a Soroban authorization entry whose nonce the host consumes when the entry is used; a second use fails on chain with Error(Auth, ExistingValue). The nonce lives under the payer's own address, for G and C accounts alike, until the signature expires. A duplicate that reaches the network is included and fails, so the sponsor still pays its fee.
threats.preconditions: A copy of a payment payload that was already sent to /settle.
threats.impact: Without protection: one wasted sponsor fee per duplicate. The payer can never be charged twice, because the host refuses the second use of the nonce.

mitigations.text: One settlement record per (network, payer, nonce), claimed before any RPC work; later requests answer from the record instead of submitting.
The settle path looks the authorization up first and answers a repeat with the recorded response, marked as a repeat.
A request whose terms differ from the recorded request is refused, never given the stored success.
Verify reads the ledger and refuses an authorization that is being settled or already was.

threats.title: Paid once, served many times
threats.threat: A buyer pays once and sends the same PAYMENT-SIGNATURE several times, concurrently or later. A stock upfront seller calls /settle without /verify; in the authorization flow, copies sent together all pass /verify before the first one settles. Either way the seller serves on a successful /settle, and an idempotent facilitator answers every repeat with the same success.
threats.stellar: Nothing Stellar-specific allows it: it follows from answering repeats with the stored result, which the x402 idempotency requirement asks for. The Stellar part is that the answer carries the one settlement transaction hash, which a seller can deduplicate on.
threats.preconditions: A seller that serves on a successful /settle without remembering which settlements it already served.
threats.impact: The seller serves a paid resource more than once for one payment. The buyer is charged once.

mitigations.text: Every repeated /settle answer carries a repeat marker in EXTENSION-RESPONSES (rail402.settlement.repeat), with the attempt id of the request that holds the settlement's claim as the repeat is answered (rail402.settlement.attempt): the one that started it, or the one that took a stale claim over and settled it, whose id replaces the abandoned request's, also for a repeat that waited through the takeover. The Bazaar never lists rail402 as an extension a resource declares.

The seller helpers refuse a second request whose settlement is a repeat or a transaction already served. Each /settle they send carries a new random attempt id, and the marker is set aside only when it echoes one of their own attempts that may have settled the payment without a success served for it (the facilitator answered settlement_pending, or /settle brought no answer of the facilitator's own: anything but its x402 settle body). That success is served once. A marked success that echoes another id (another seller, replica, an earlier run, or a request that took over a stale claim), no id, or an id already resumed is refused, whatever the timing; a refusal in the facilitator's own x402 body waits for nothing, and a refused repeat never counts as the serve.
In the authorization flow, verify refuses an authorization that is being settled or was, so a copy sent after the first settlement started never reaches the handler.

The demo seller settles every route and tool, exact and upto, through withSettleDedupe, and so do the Playground's lab sellers; the seller quickstart, the HTTP seller example and the seller helpers page wrap their facilitator client the same way, in both flows.
The Playground's lab sellers wrap their facilitator client in withSettleDedupe inside the trace recorder, so a refused copy is traced as refused.

threats.title: An upto authorization settled for zero stays usable
threats.threat: A seller settles an upto payment for zero, then tries to charge the same authorization again for a positive amount.
threats.stellar: An on-chain zero settlement still uses the payer's authorization entry, so the host consumes its nonce like any other settlement. An off-chain zero (UPTO_ZERO_SETTLEMENT=offchain) sends nothing, so the nonce stays unused on chain until the signature expires.
threats.preconditions: An upto payment settled for zero.
threats.impact: Without protection, a second settlement of the same authorization for up to the cap.

mitigations.text: The upto contract consumes the payer's nonce for a zero settlement too.

An off-chain zero is a terminal record in the settlement ledger, so a later request for any amount is answered from it or refused as a conflict; only the named authority can settle on chain, and it is Rail402's.

A database restore can discard that record while the authorization is still valid, so every restore is recorded (restore-dump.sh in its own transaction, creating the table for an older dump; the runbook after a point-in-time recovery; the migration that adds the record, for a database that already holds settlements or was migrated earlier). Every upto network, whatever its zero settlement mode and ledger time now, then verifies no upto payment and settles none that moves funds until the chain has passed the longest window rule 7 can accept (the largest maxTimeoutSeconds at the shortest ledger time it counts, one second), counted from a ledger recorded only by recordRestoreHold (the service's network poll): the ledger the chain can have reached by the time of a reading from a provider of that network whose newest ledger closed within the last minute (that ledger plus one per second since). Requests never record or move it and, until it is recorded, hold from their own reading. The poll starts the hold again from a reset test network's new chain only after corroborating the reset (the same checks and a second poll), and never on pubnet.

threats.residual: With off-chain zeros and STORE=memory, a restart forgets the record; the authorization then stays settleable by Rail402's own authority until it expires. Use Postgres wherever off-chain zeros are enabled. The hold after a restore is counted in ledgers from the current TIMEOUT_MAX_SECONDS at the shortest ledger time rule 7 counts, so no ledger time setting, before or after the restore, shortens it. Lowering TIMEOUT_MAX_SECONDS in the same restore does, and so could a point-in-time recovery the operator did not record, a failover to an asynchronous standby that lost recent commits (not recorded at all), rolling back to a release that predates the record without waiting out the hold, or the runtime role setting the recorded ledger to 0 or deleting the record on a one-role host (it can change that ledger on any host, as it could already reopen an off-chain zero by deleting its settlement row): an authorization could then be settled once more, never above its cap and only to its payTo. The first ledger is recorded from one provider's reading that passed the passphrase and freshness checks (its newest ledger closed within the last minute, and not in the future), as that ledger plus one for every second since it closed, the most the chain can have reached by then, so an honest reading up to a minute old cannot set it too low; until it is recorded every upto request holds, and rail402_upto_restore_hold_pending shows it. A provider that lies (compromised or misconfigured), answering this network's passphrase with a fresh-looking ledger far below the chain, can still record a low first ledger and void the hold on any network, pubnet included; on a test network it can also restart the hold early over two polls. Configure only providers you trust; an in-process facilitator that never runs recordRestoreHold stays held after a restore until the owner records the ledger.

threats.title: A copied exact authorization lands first
threats.threat: Someone who sees the settlement envelope (the seller, an RPC operator, a validator's pending queue) copies the payer's authorization entry into a transaction of their own and gets it included before Rail402's.
threats.stellar: A Soroban authorization is a bearer instrument for exactly one invocation: whoever submits it can only make the signed transfer happen, from the payer to payTo for the signed amount. It cannot be redirected. Rail402's own transaction then fails on the consumed nonce and its fee is spent.
threats.preconditions: Access to the envelope between signing and inclusion, and an account to pay the copy's fee.
threats.impact: One wasted sponsor fee per event. The attacker pays its own fee and gains nothing; the payment settles as signed.

mitigations.text: Rail402 submits as soon as the settle-time simulation passes, which leaves little time to copy the entry.
Signed envelopes and authorizations are redacted from logs.
Wasted fees are counted, so griefing is visible and bounded by the hourly budget.

threats.title: The seller is told the payment failed although it settled
threats.threat: After a front-run, Rail402's transaction fails with a consumed nonce and the seller is told the payment failed, although the payer was charged. Likewise when Rail402's rebroadcast is refused and someone else lands its public transaction in a fee bump of their own.
threats.stellar: The chain holds the proof: the nonce entry's last-modified ledger, and in that ledger a successful transaction whose address credential (payer, nonce, signature expiration) and root invocation are byte-equal to the payer's signed entry, with the matching token transfer event.
threats.preconditions: A front-run as in F1, or a refused rebroadcast of a settlement transaction a send may have exposed.
threats.impact: Without reconciliation the seller withholds a resource that was paid for.

mitigations.text: A failed settlement whose nonce was consumed is reconciled: Rail402 finds the other transaction on chain, proves it carried the same signed invocation after the request was claimed, and answers success with its hash.
Proof requires a byte-equal root invocation and credential; a different invocation for the same nonce stays a failure.

The failure is kept only when the search read RPCs that have reached the ledger Rail402's transaction failed in and hold the ledger that consumed the nonce; a read from a lagging provider, a backend behind a balancer or another provider after a failover, a backend whose history starts after the consuming ledger, or a read error, leaves the settlement open for the next pass, which reads the failure again and searches with fresh reads. One that stays undecided for a minute is reported as unresolvable, and a failure on the used nonce whose nonce reads unused at the ledger it failed in (its entry lapsed) is reported as unresolvable at once instead of kept.

An upto settlement whose rebroadcast the network refuses for good (a frozen sponsor key, say) after a send may have exposed its transaction keeps waiting until no later ledger can include that transaction, since anyone can wrap it in a fee bump of their own until then; the inner-hash lookup finds such a landing and the payment is answered as settled. One whose sends were all refused finishes at once.

An exact settlement included after the payer's authorization expired is searched the same way: the host checks the expiration before the nonce, so a copy that landed before the expiration makes Rail402's transaction fail as expired, and the payment is answered as settled with the copy's hash.

An exact settlement whose own transaction the network refused for good, or can never apply because another transaction took its channel's sequence number, is decided from the payer's nonce, never at once: anyone who holds the payment can carry its authorization in a transaction of their own until it expires. A copy that landed is answered as settled with its hash, and the settlement is answered as failed only once the authorization expired unused, so a seller is never told to refuse a buyer, or a buyer to pay again, while the first payment can still land.

An exact settlement whose own transaction was included and failed for a cause that does not end the authorization (a balance spent, a trustline removed or deauthorized, an account or smart account that refused it for now, a token error, a failure without diagnostics) is not finished either: the failure rolls back, the payer's nonce included, so anyone who holds the payment can still land it until it expires. An expired-authorization error ends it only when the transaction failed past the payer's own expiration ledger, since a contract in the call path or a shorter-lived entry can raise one. The settlement answers settlement_pending, gives its channel back at once, and is searched as above; it is answered with its on-chain cause, the fee counted as wasted, once the nonce reads unused past the expiration. The SDK reports those causes as paid unknown, never retryable, so a buyer is not invited to pay again while the first payment can still land.

mitigations.text: An HTTP resource, or an MCP tool at an http(s) endpoint, is published only after its own 402 (for a tool, the answer to an unpaid tools/call over MCP) confirms payTo, price and metadata; what is published always comes from that answer, so echoed metadata never changes a listing on its own.
MCP tools are asked through safe-fetch with the MCP client: the tool must be declared in tools/list and its unpaid call must answer with the x402 PaymentRequired.

A published listing is decided by one answer only, at its resource or its route template's example path, asked as its origin confirmed it, and a published MCP tool by its listed call; an answer at a path a payer chose never changes or withdraws it, a published tool whose listed call fails for now is retried without calling it with a payload's arguments, and an example kept from before examples were confirmed never withdraws it. While a listing not yet listed has a check open, the check keeps up to 4 paths per asset (the largest payments) and 8 in all (the latest) that its owner's payers paid, asks them largest payments first within its host's budget, going on from what earlier runs found when the budget runs out, and lists the listing from an answer that lists it for its owner at that answer's price first. Later settlements never reset a check's retries; one that pays the owner of a listing not yet listed makes its check due now and has its path asked again, and a run it makes due before the next scheduled retry spends none.

threats.title: Taking over another seller's listing
threats.threat: An attacker pays a URL that belongs to another seller, but to its own payTo, to take over or modify that listing.
threats.stellar: The settled payTo is the only identity the facilitator has proven, from a settlement that moved value to it. An upto zero moves nothing and proves nothing, so it never catalogs.
threats.preconditions: A settlement for the victim's URL to the attacker's account.
threats.impact: Payments for a listed resource redirected to the attacker.

mitigations.text: A listing is bound to the settled payTo; another payTo is refused with bazaar_owner_conflict, and ownership moves only when the origin names the new payTo.

A settlement that moved nothing (an upto zero, on-chain or off) never catalogs. A settlement that moved one base unit does not help either: a listing is published only with what its own origin answers (P1, P9).

Every claimant of a listing is kept until a check ran with it, a check only claims asked for never withdraws a published listing, and a claim is weighed at the listing's resource or route-template example path alone, never at the path the claimant paid: the listing moves only to a claimant that path names, and not its owner. A template's example is the path its creating settlement paid, then the one its origin confirmed when it was listed, never pathParams a payer echoed; any other answer there refuses the claim.

threats.title: Wash settlements to flood or rank the catalog
threats.threat: A seller pays itself through a second account many times to create many listings or to look popular.
threats.stellar: Settlements are cheap on Stellar, so volume is a weak signal of quality.
threats.preconditions: Two accounts and a little USDC.
threats.impact: Catalog spam and manipulated rankings.

mitigations.text: New listings are rate-limited per owner and origin, per payer and for the whole catalog.

The owner's and the network's hourly quotas are spent when a listing is first published: one its origin confirms while either is spent waits, without spending a retry, so listings created at once or kept pending for hours never publish past the quotas.

Tools no origin can confirm (mcp://) are counted apart, within half of the network's hourly quota of new listings and half of its room, so dust payments for them never use up what sellers with an origin need.

threats.title: Planting a seller's MCP tool listing
threats.threat: A payer pays a seller's payTo one base unit (or settles one unit under an upto cap of any size) while echoing the seller's MCP endpoint and tool name with its own description, input schema or price, hoping to publish, freeze or domain-verify that content under the seller's identity, or to use up the seller's quota of new listings.
threats.stellar: The settlement proves a payment to payTo, not who wrote the echoed tool description. Dust costs the payer almost nothing and the sponsor pays the fee, so a settlement alone cannot vouch for content.
threats.preconditions: A trustline and one base unit of the asset; the seller's MCP endpoint and tool name.
threats.impact: Spoofed tool descriptions (prompt injection) and prices shown to agents under the seller's verified identity; the seller's own tools not cataloged.

mitigations.text: A tool at an http(s) endpoint stays pending until the tool itself answers an unpaid tools/call with a PaymentRequired naming the owner; until an origin check has confirmed it, the tool must also offer the scheme, network, asset, payTo and price (cap) of a settlement for it, the one that created it or one its check keeps, or the listing is quarantined with origin_payment_mismatch. A later settlement never narrows what an earlier one proved.

A later settlement the tool itself asked for is checked again and replaces planted content with the tool's own answer to its listed call; a planted settlement can neither change nor withdraw a confirmed tool whose listed call answers with a PaymentRequired or fails for now. Once that call is answered without one, the first call a payer proposed, largest payments first, whose PaymentRequired lists the tool for its owner updates the tool with the tool's own answer to that call, and the example that answer declares becomes the listed call (the payer's arguments when the tool echoes them; the change then stays until that call is answered without a PaymentRequired).

A check calls the tool as its listing describes first; the example arguments its settlements proposed are tried only when that call is answered without a PaymentRequired (a published tool whose listed call fails for now is retried instead), and only a PaymentRequired to them that lists the tool for its owner is used, so echoed arguments can confirm a tool but never withdraw it: only the listed call's answer does.
Domain trust is granted only to origin-verified listings, and needs the two-way SEP-1 binding.
The owner's hourly quota is kept per origin, and only listings that origin confirmed for a settlement that paid the owner its price count toward it.

threats.title: A tampered payment or a false settlement report
threats.threat: A scheme client changes the payload after the guard approved it, or a seller reports a settlement that did not happen, reports another payment's transaction hash, or settles through its own contract so the transaction does not look like a direct settlement.
threats.stellar: The host records every authorization nonce it consumes in a temporary ledger entry keyed by the payer and the nonce, and only the entry the payer signed can consume it. A transaction used a payment's authorization exactly when it carries the payer's entry with that payment's nonce and its meta creates that nonce entry, whatever its call path: Soroban matches an entry below the top-level call, so a wrapper, router or batch contract can settle it too, and one transaction can consume several nonces. A transfer event alone says nothing about which authorization moved the money.
threats.preconditions: A malicious scheme client or seller.
threats.impact: Paying for something else, believing a payment failed or succeeded wrongly, or a session budget that under-counts what moved.

mitigations.text: The guard compares the payload with what it signed.

A payment is proven only by its own nonce: a transaction that consumed it settles the reservation whatever its shape, for the exact price, or for upto the amount the signed settlement contract recorded for the signed terms (the whole cap when that cannot be read). A consumed authorization is never released.

A reported hash is only a claim against the payment it was reported for and counts as spent; it never removes a transaction from another payment's proof. Budget returns only when the authorization has expired and no transaction in its validity range consumed it.
An expired payment the RPC can no longer prove either way counts as spent at its whole amount and is no longer reconciled.

threats.title: Channel sequence collisions
threats.threat: Two settlements use the same channel account at once, or something else uses a channel's key, and transactions fail with a bad sequence number.
threats.stellar: An account's transactions are ordered by sequence number; one in-flight transaction per source is the rule.
threats.preconditions: Concurrency, several replicas, or external use of a channel key.
threats.impact: Failed settlements and wasted fees.

mitigations.text: Channels are leased exclusively through Postgres across replicas.
Sequence conflicts are counted so external use is visible.

Every call of the service's own RPC clients fails after 10 seconds; upstream's exact verifier, whose client has no timeout, is cut off after the same 10 seconds with a retryable unexpected_verify_error; and a settlement that has signed nothing by the end of its 30-second claim window signs nothing afterwards, which also bounds upstream's settlement client, so a hung provider can never let a lease expire under a settlement that may still sign.
RPC clients carry a call timeout below the claim and lease windows.
A channel referenced by an open settlement is never leased again, whether its lease was released or expired, unless the settlement gave it back because its bytes can never apply.

A settlement refused with txBadSeq gives its channel back at once, once the channel's sequence number on the network has reached the transaction's and neither its hash nor its inner hash landed (read from an RPC that has ingested that ledger and retains every ledger since the claim): its bytes can never apply, so the channel is quarantined for SETTLE_CHANNEL_QUARANTINE_MS, doubled for each further conflict in a row, instead of being held until the payment expires or reused at once. The settlement is marked as having given the channel back, so the channel pool may lease it again while the settlement's outcome waits, and finishing the settlement releases nothing. An upto settlement then finishes with nothing charged; an exact one when the payer's authorization expired unused, or as settled through a copy of it (F2).

A quarantined channel is not leased by any replica until its cooldown passes, and when it is, a channel whose account sequence number moved since the conflict is quarantined again instead of settling.

A conflict decided at once reads the payer's nonce, and when a send may have been accepted or the payment is exact the inner hash too, from an RPC at or past the ledger of the sequence proof; a lagging or switched provider leaves the settlement waiting (rpc_behind), so an authorization another transaction carried is never reported as unused.

threats.threat: A recorded settlement is examined after the RPC no longer keeps the ledgers that could prove it included or absent, or by an RPC that has not ingested them yet.
threats.stellar: An RPC keeps only a limited window of recent ledgers and transactions; older ones cannot be read from it. Providers, and the backends behind one provider's balancer, reach each ledger at different times, so consecutive reads can come from different heights.

threats.title: The relay used to reach private networks or as an open proxy
threats.threat: A visitor, or a script calling the Playground's API, asks the relay to fetch a loopback, private or cloud-metadata address, a name that resolves to one, or a seller that redirects to one; or uses the relay to send volume to third parties from the Playground's address.
threats.stellar: Nothing Stellar-specific: the relay exists because Rail402 and most x402 sellers answer no CORS headers, so a page cannot call them itself. A paid request through it carries a PAYMENT-SIGNATURE the visitor's own key made.
threats.preconditions: Network access to the Playground server.
threats.impact: Without protection: requests into the server's network, or the Playground's address used for abuse.

mitigations.text: The relay sends with safe-fetch under a fixed policy: https on port 443 to public addresses only, DNS answers checked and pinned, redirects refused except same-origin hops for unpaid probes, request and answer size limits.

By host name, it never contacts the Playground itself (its public host and the platform's generated domain), the facilitator, the Bazaar, the other host names of that service (a facilitator at testnet.<domain> also denies mainnet., pubnet. and explorer.<domain>) or an operator-denied host.
Per-client, global, per-host, in-flight and daily byte limits, with Retry-After, and a switch to turn the relay off.

Global limits are fair-shared: one network (an IPv4 address or an IPv6 /48) holds at most an eighth of a pool, or its per-client limit when that is larger; clients are keyed by IPv4 address or IPv6 /56.

Only a payment that decodes as an x402 payment counts against the paid limits, whether it travels in PAYMENT-SIGNATURE or in an MCP tool call's _meta; anything else is refused before a token is taken.

The demo seller has a paid pool of its own, a paid request that reached no seller gives the shared pool its token back, and the lab sellers return it when the facilitator was never asked, so payments that only have the right shape cannot use up the pools the demo flows need.

Unpaid requests wait no longer than the SDK's probe timeouts; bodies pass only as JSON, text or octet-stream; slots of an abandoned upload or an unread answer are released; connections to hosts other than the demo seller are closed as soon as each answer's body ends, even when the seller never read the upload or keeps sending after a compressed body, and a redirect's without waiting for its body.
Unpaid requests and answer bytes are also limited per network, bytes for all clients per day, requests in flight per destination host, and each network gets at most its share of a host's budget.

threats.stellar: The relay holds no key and no session, so a forged request carries no authority the attacker lacks; a payment needs a signature from the key in the Playground's own page.

The Bazaar and /supported proxies refuse another site's requests the same way, so no page can spend their shared upstream budget through visitors' browsers.

threats.title: Dust self-payments drain the pubnet fee budget for every seller
threats.threat: A caller settles many valid payments of the smallest amount, often to a payTo it controls, so the sponsor pays a full fee each time and the hourly budget is spent for everyone.
threats.stellar: A token transfer settlement costs the sponsor a resource fee of tens of thousands of stroops, while the payment can be one base unit; paying oneself is legal on chain.
threats.preconditions: One funded account with a trustline; on pubnet an API key when keys are required.
threats.impact: Without controls the hourly budget is exhausted within minutes and every other seller's settlements are refused until the hour moves on.

mitigations.text: Each access key carries its own hourly sponsor budget, keyless callers share one, and both are checked with the network budget when the settlement is claimed.
Pubnet requires an explicit minimum amount for every accepted asset and refuses to start without one.

Per-payer and per-payTo settlement limits per minute, on by default on pubnet, count only payments that proved the payer's signature (just before the sponsor signs), so forged payloads naming a seller or a wallet cannot use up its quota. The payTo limit is counted per access key, with one shared count for keyless callers, so keyless dust cannot use up a keyed seller's quota.
On pubnet a non-zero upto settlement is held to the asset's minimum, as an exact amount is; a zero settles off-chain.
Finished settlements count the fee actually charged against the budgets (nothing when they expired or the network refused them), so payloads that never land stop holding budget once finished.

mitigations.text: A payer whose settlements were included and failed PAYER_FAILURES_PER_HOUR times in the last hour is refused with a coded, retryable reason until the hour moves on (3 by default on pubnet).
Pubnet's expiration margin defaults to two ledgers, so a settlement that lands a ledger late does not fail after the fee is paid.

mitigations.text: Before the body is read, a /verify or /settle with a usable access key is charged to a bucket of that key on every host, never to its client address: keyless traffic of either network, unknown paths and refused requests from the same address or IPv6 /64 never spend it. The bucket holds what the key may send a minute on all its networks, and at least RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE, so the key's own per-network limits are what refuse it. A request whose network does not admit the key pays its address's bucket as well, so a key never carries keyless payments past the address's limit.
Once the network and caller are known, each network applies its own limit: per key on pubnet, never the testnet address bucket.
A held or starting network refuses only its own requests.

The responses of a connection, including those the server gives without reaching the app, must be handed to the operating system's socket buffer within RESPONSE_WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS of being ready, and one connection may have at most MAX_PIPELINED_REQUESTS requests waiting for their answers, on every route; otherwise the connection is reset and every response it held released. A response's clock starts once it and every response before it on the connection are ready, so a pipelined backlog shares one deadline and the time handlers take to answer never counts.

A discovery request keeps its admission slot until its response has been handed to the client's connection, so the slots bound the discovery pages the process keeps for clients that have not taken them, and one client (an address, or a forwarded client of a discovery-internal key) holds at most DISCOVERY_MAX_IN_FLIGHT_PER_CLIENT requests of a lane.

threats.title: The shared database pool is exhausted by testnet work
threats.threat: Testnet settlements, cataloging and limiter writes hold every connection in the one pool, so pubnet settlement claims wait or fail.

mitigations.text: With several networks served, pubnet's settlement ledger and channel leases use a connection pool of their own.
Pubnet's request limit, per-payer and per-payTo limits and metering use that pool too, routed by network.

On the pubnet host (PUBLIC_HOSTS), and in a process that serves pubnet alone, the service-wide limit decides the key in memory first: a key pubnet admits is limited on pubnet's pool (the one pool when pubnet is served alone), every other caller in the process only, so no pubnet /verify or /settle on the pubnet host waits for a shared connection to be admitted and no anonymous caller's per-address limit there takes a connection of the pool pubnet's settlements use; where pubnet requires keys, such a caller is refused before any database work. With the Bazaar the discovery routes keep their limits on the discovery pools; without it a /discovery/ path is limited like any other.
Pubnet's account provisioning and upto contract TTL rounds take their sponsor lock through pubnet's pool.
The public, unlimited /metrics answers from memory: channels in use is counted every second in the background, one count per network at a time, so scrapes never take a database connection.

The runtime role's connection limit must hold every pool of every replica: the service reads it at startup, logs how many replicas it holds, and with pubnet refuses to start below one process's pools, so anonymous load on the shared and discovery pools never takes the role's slots that pubnet's pool and readiness need.

A client already over its limit is refused from memory, without another write, until its window ends (measured from a monotonic clock read before the refused write, so never longer); only requests already on their way to the database when its first refusal comes back still write.
Every pool fails a query after DATABASE_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT_MS without a connection, so pubnet's fail-closed limiters refuse with a code instead of queueing without end.
Reconciliation runs per network, one round at a time per network; a network whose ledger or RPC fails or hangs never holds up another network's round.

The public /ready probes the database through one connection of its own, at most once every 2 seconds, and concurrent requests share the running probe, so a readiness flood never takes a connection from settlements and a queue for the shared pool is never reported as an outage.

threats.title: One leaked seed controls the sponsor, every channel and the authority

mitigations.text: Pubnet startup reads the sponsor's signers and thresholds and refuses (or holds pubnet) unless the hot key meets medium but not high and the configured cold signer (PUBNET_SPONSOR_COLD_SIGNER) alone reaches high.

The cold signer must be the only way to high: keys derived from the sponsor seed (channels, the upto authority) may not be signers, and the hot key with every other signer, pre-authorized transaction, hash-x and signed-payload signers included, stays below high.

The leak response starts with the cold key: a reviewed, unsigned transaction from the cold account (its source and fee payer) sets the hot key's weight to 0 on the sponsor (high threshold, cold key only), so the leaked key cannot block it through the sponsor's sequence; a separate cold-signed sweep follows. The owner's quota is kept per origin (scheme, host and port), so listings an attacker's host confirms for the payTo count only at that host and never against the seller's own origins.

A listing counts toward its owner's quota only once its origin confirmed a settlement that paid the owner its price there (for upto, the whole cap), and never after an ownership transfer; none is charged past the quota, and one that would be waits to be published. threats.title: Expensive searches
threats.threat: Unauthenticated searches each run an embedding on the CPU that settlement also needs; a flood of distinct queries, within the service-wide request limit, keeps the model busy.
threats.stellar: Pubnet settlements share the process, so search load delays real-money payments.
threats.preconditions: Many distinct queries from one client or many clients.
threats.impact: Without protection: slow searches and settlements for everyone.

mitigations.text: A per-client cost bucket for discovery: an uncached search costs more than a cached one, deep offsets cost more than the first page.
A bounded least-recently-used query-embedding cache, so repeated queries run no model.
An embedder concurrency cap: a query that finds the model busy is answered lexical-only, as partial results, instead of queueing.

threats.title: Search index snapshots exhaust memory
threats.threat: Catalog growth on either network, catalog changes and cursor requests make the search index hold more memory than the process has: every listing's content in every snapshot, many snapshots alive for their cursor lifetime, or listings written to maximise the index's size.
threats.stellar: Testnet catalog churn is free, and the process also serves pubnet.
threats.preconditions: Many listings (free on testnet for originless mcp:// tools), frequent catalog changes, and a search with a cursor after each.
threats.impact: Without protection: memory growth until the process is killed, interrupting both networks.

mitigations.text: A snapshot keeps only what ranking and filters read; a result page reads its listings from the catalog. The catalog is read in batches with a statement timeout, so a build never holds every listing's content.

Each field indexes a bounded number of terms, and each network's listings may take a bounded share of a snapshot (unverified listings at most half), so free testnet listings never push pubnet out of search.
Count and byte caps on kept snapshots, oldest superseded first (their cursors expire), with estimates calibrated against measured heap, and metrics for the snapshots and for listings left out.
Each network holds a bounded number of published listings, and listings no origin confirmed (and, where set, idle ones) expire after their last settlement.

threats.title: Discovery beyond capacity starves settlement and health checks
threats.threat: Discovery requests arriving faster than the process completes them (uncached searches over a large catalog, from many addresses, each within its own cost budget) pile up inside the process: every one waits for a database connection of the pool settlement uses, the event loop falls behind, and /health, /ready and /settle wait behind them; searches fail with 500 after the pool's acquire timeout or hang until the client gives up.
threats.stellar: One process serves testnet and pubnet: free testnet discovery load must never delay real-money pubnet settlements or take a network out of its load balancer.
threats.preconditions: A request rate above the discovery throughput the process reaches (measured with the load-test package), spread over enough addresses to stay within the per-client limits.
threats.impact: Without protection: settlement, health and readiness slow down or time out for every network, and discovery answers with uncoded 500s.

mitigations.text: Load shedding ahead of every limit and database read: at most DISCOVERY_MAX_IN_FLIGHT discovery requests run at once and DISCOVERY_QUEUE_LENGTH wait, each at most DISCOVERY_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_MS; the rest are refused at once with 503 discovery_overloaded and Retry-After, counted in rail402_discovery_shed_total.

Discovery reads the catalog and keeps its per-address and internal-identity limits through a database pool of its own (DISCOVERY_DATABASE_POOL_SIZE connections, DISCOVERY_DATABASE_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT_MS), so it never holds a connection settlement, limits, metering or readiness need.

The search index is built through a pool of its own (SEARCH_INDEX_POOL_SIZE connections, DISCOVERY_DATABASE_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT_MS) that no request takes, so discovery load never holds a connection an index build needs.
A busy or unreachable catalog database is answered with a coded 503 (discovery_overloaded, discovery_catalog_unavailable) and Retry-After, never a 500.
A result page reuses listings read within the revision read interval at the same catalog revision, so repeated results cost no database read.
/health never does I/O, /ready/<network> answers from the last poll, and /ready answers from the last database probe while a new one runs.
Sustained shedding raises a ticket (Rail402DiscoveryShedding) naming the reason, so refused searches do not go unnoticed.

threats.title: A pubnet budget that renews forever or resets, or caps set too high
threats.threat: The default budget window renews when it expires, so a looping or prompt-injected agent spends its full budget every day with no end; or an owner configures caps far above what an agent should ever pay with real funds.
threats.stellar: Every pubnet payment moves real USDC from the agent's account under a Soroban authorization the agent signs on its own; nothing on chain limits how often a funded key signs.
threats.preconditions: An agent with a pubnet key runs unattended for longer than one budget window, or its caps were set carelessly.
threats.impact: Real funds spent beyond what the owner meant, one window after another.

mitigations.text: On pubnet the default budget window does not renew; renewal is an explicit choice (autoRenew, RAIL402_SESSION_AUTO_RENEW).

Pubnet USDC caps above 1 USDC per call or 10 USDC per window, and caps on any other pubnet asset (which has no built-in ceiling), are refused unless larger caps are allowed explicitly (allowLargeCaps, RAIL402_ALLOW_LARGE_CAPS).

A pubnet buyer with a key keeps its budget in the persistent SQLite store: RAIL402_BUDGET_STORE=memory is refused there, since every process start and every restart of rail402-mcp would open a fresh window with the full budget.

threats.title: A pubnet payment is signed without a human, or an approval covers more than it showed
threats.threat: An agent, steered by listing text or a prompt, makes a real-money payment with nobody confirming the network, recipient and amount; or it reuses one approval to pay other recipients or listings, or shows the person a resource text that hides what is really paid.
threats.stellar: The buyer signs a Soroban authorization entry that lets the facilitator move the stated amount to payTo; once signed and settled, the transfer is final.
threats.preconditions: A pubnet key configured in the SDK, CLI or MCP server.
threats.impact: A real payment the owner never saw.

mitigations.text: A pubnet buyer with a signer must choose how payments are confirmed: a confirm function (SDK), a form elicitation through the MCP client or RAIL402_MCP_CONFIRM=never for headless agents (MCP server). Under first-per-session an approval covers only the window, recipient base account, listing (or resource without one), asset, scheme and settlement authority it was shown for; any other one is asked about again. A declined or unavailable confirmation signs and reserves nothing.

Every prompt says what approving covers: this payment only, or that recipient and listing again without asking, up to the per-call cap and the budget left, until the window ends. It shows the listing and the upto settlement authority, and untrusted fields stay on one line without control, line-break or bidirectional characters; an MCP endpoint whose raw text carries them is refused (egress_url_invalid), and the normalized URL is what is confirmed and reserved.

The sealed MCP intent binds the listing, the upto settlement authority and the budget window with the network, scheme, asset, recipient, resource and amount, so a retry that names another authority or listing, or whose payment falls in another window (it renewed, or the session was restarted, while the person decided), is asked about again with that window's end and budget.

An MCP confirmation's request state carries a single-use id and a digest of the exact tool call it was asked for: a replayed approval is refused with rpc_confirmation_used, one reused for other arguments or another tool with rpc_confirmation_mismatch, and a forged or expired state fails its MAC check; so under RAIL402_MCP_CONFIRM=every one approval signs at most one payment.

No helper defaults a pubnet buyer to never asking: openBuyer (CLI) and openConfiguredBuyer (MCP) pass no confirmation policy unless given one, so the SDK refuses a pubnet buyer with a key until the caller chooses.

The CLI asks on the terminal before a pubnet payment (each process is its own buyer, so each pay or purchase asks), or takes --yes. This protects a person at the terminal from mistakes; it is not a control against an agent that can run the CLI, which can pass --yes or answer its own terminal. Agents get confirmation through rail402-mcp's elicitation, which the MCP client shows to the person, and are otherwise bounded by caps, tagged keys and the policy.

threats.title: A testnet key used on pubnet, or a key for the wrong network
threats.threat: A key handled as a throwaway testnet key (in examples, shell history, Playground exports) pays on pubnet, or a server meant for one network is given the other network's key.
threats.stellar: A Stellar seed is a valid key on every network, so nothing in the key itself says which network it belongs to.
threats.preconditions: A key file or a seed in the environment, and a pubnet configuration.
threats.impact: Real funds paid with a key that was never protected as a real-money key.

mitigations.text: Key files carry a network tag (rail402 keys new/import write it); a file tagged for another network is refused, pubnet refuses untagged files unless explicitly allowed, and a seed in RAIL402_SECRET_KEY is never used on pubnet.

The Playground's key download is a key file tagged for testnet, and rail402 keys import reads a tagged file and refuses a tag for another network (key_network_mismatch), so a browser key never becomes a pubnet key unseen.

threats.title: An agent pointed at an impostor Bazaar or MCP endpoint
threats.threat: An agent is configured, or talked into using, a hostile catalog or discovery endpoint that lists attacker recipients at plausible prices.
threats.stellar: A listing names the payTo a payment authorization will credit; whoever controls the catalog chooses which Stellar accounts an agent is shown.
threats.preconditions: A buyer configured with an untrusted Bazaar URL, or an agent that follows listing IDs from an untrusted discovery endpoint.
threats.impact: Payments to an attacker's account, within the caps.

mitigations.text: Pubnet needs an explicit https Bazaar URL; the hosted endpoint never pays, so a listing found anywhere is paid only through the buyer's own Bazaar, whose live 402 must match the listing's owner and price (M5).

A pubnet buyer built in code gets the same rule: createBuyer and createBrowserBuyer refuse a Bazaar or facilitator URL that is not https, carries credentials, or names an IP address, localhost, a single label or a private-network suffix (payment_policy_invalid).

Hosted mode is dispatched before anything else loads and is built only on @rail402.dev/sdk/discovery: a running hosted process never loads the SDK's key loading, signing guard, budget ledgers, payment flows or scheme clients, nor the local server's payment tools; a test records the process's module graph and fails if any appears.

threats.title: Hosted MCP calls used to flood discovery
threats.threat: A remote client loops tool calls, each a search, to load the Bazaar and the host shared with settlement.
threats.stellar: Search runs in the service that also verifies and settles Stellar payments, so its cost competes with settlement.
threats.preconditions: A public hosted endpoint.
threats.impact: Slower or refused discovery and settlement.

mitigations.text: Per-client limit (IPv4 address or IPv6 /64), an in-flight cap answered with rpc_overloaded, a 64 KiB body limit, at most 10 results per search, a 3 s upstream timeout, and no sessions.
One request carries one JSON-RPC message: a batch is refused with rpc_batch_unsupported before any tool runs, so the per-client limit and the in-flight cap bound tool calls, not just HTTP requests.
A process-wide budget of tool calls per minute (RAIL402_MCP_UPSTREAM_PER_MINUTE, default 300, each at most one Bazaar request) answers rpc_upstream_budget itself.

With a Bazaar discovery-internal access key (read from the file named by RAIL402_MCP_UPSTREAM_KEY_FILE, never from the environment, never logged), every upstream request carries the key and an X-Rail402-Client identifier per remote client (an HMAC of its address key under the access key), so the Bazaar budgets each remote client apart instead of charging every hosted user to the endpoint's address.

At the Bazaar, a hosted endpoint that calls with a discovery-internal key and its client in X-Rail402-Client is charged per client: each remote client has its own discovery cost budget (SEARCH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE units, as large as a direct client's) within the identity's own, so one client cannot use up the others' searches.
TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS has no default, so a deployment must state its proxy chain; X-Forwarded-For arriving while it is 0 is logged once and counted in rail402_mcp_warnings_total.

threats.title: Tampered or truncated ledger data
threats.threat: Ledger bytes from the public data lake or Lumeus RPC are altered, swapped, replayed or invented, planting or hiding settlements.
threats.stellar: Each ledger header commits to the previous ledger's hash, to its transaction set and to its results. Metas are not hashed by the header, but a successful contract call's result records the SHA-256 of its return value and events, so events are bound to consensus through the result.
threats.preconditions: Control of, or a man in the middle on, a ledger source.
threats.impact: Without protection: invented or missing settlements that look rebuildable.

mitigations.text: Every ledger read must hash to its own header, its transaction set and results must match the header's hashes, and it must be the ledger asked for; a failure marks the ledger failed and stops the indexer. The full-scan rebuild also requires each ledger's previous hash to be the last verified ledger's hash.

Before reading a successful candidate's events, the classifier recomputes SHA-256 of InvokeHostFunctionSuccessPreImage { returnValue, events } from the meta and requires the operation result's success hash; a mismatch stops the indexer (events_unbound). The upto event must also equal the signed settle(payer, terms, amount) arguments.

Independent anchors: the indexer commits a ledger, so serves and reports its rows, only after its hash matched a Horizon with full history (required on pubnet); a different hash marks the ledger failed and stops the indexer, and the anchors checked are stored and listed in the published manifest. The rebuild checks every anchor it is given and refuses one it cannot check.
Lumeus RPC getLedgers answers are checked ledger by ledger: each ledger's own header must name the sequence it is listed under.
The data lake reader is pinned to one https host, refuses redirects, caps object and decompressed sizes, and checks each object holds exactly the ledger asked for.
The report covers the range only up to the first candidate ledger that is not indexed yet or failed, says where and why it stops, and is not marked reproducible while a ledger is failed.
A live lookup is answered only when the RPC's envelope hashes (outer, or inner for a fee bump) on the network include the requested hash; otherwise explorer_lookup_unavailable.

threats.title: Gaps, epochs and lag hide or duplicate rows
threats.threat: A missed range, a testnet reset that reuses ledger numbers, a replayed or broken discovery walk, a bounded run that ends before ledgers already found, a rebuilt discovery index, or a stalled tail makes the Explorer silently incomplete, double-counts rows or merges two epochs.
threats.stellar: Testnet resets start ledger numbers again; transaction hashes include the network passphrase, which testnet keeps.
threats.preconditions: A testnet reset, a crash or failure mid-walk, a second indexer on the same database, a bounded run, a registry change, or a discovery index rebuild.
threats.impact: Without protection: wrong totals with no visible sign.

mitigations.text: Rows are keyed by (network, epoch, transaction hash) and written as upserts. A testnet reset is a new discovery generation whose head is more than 1,000 ledgers behind the indexed candidates: it stops the indexer before anything of the new network is stored, until the new epoch is registered; a head that is only behind (a lagging replica, or a source without a new generation) and anything on pubnet is counted and logged, never a stop. A bounded run that cannot discover or read a ledger through its end exits non-zero (range_incomplete).

Every discovery page's candidate ledgers and the checkpoint it vouches for (the ledger before its last record, or scanned_through_ledger at the end of a window; records must come in ascending order) are stored in one transaction, so a failure loses at most the page under way; candidates are upserts, the checkpoint only moves forward, and a ledger is committed only while it is pending, so a restart or a second indexer never loses or repeats one.

Routes keep their registry bounds only: a bounded run's last ledger bounds its walks and is never stored, so a later run resumes where it stopped; a registry range that ends before a route's checkpoint moves the checkpoint back to its end, so a widened range is walked again.
A discovery answer under another generation or decoder than the route's last page walks the route again from its first ledger, so records the source added or corrected in a rebuild are found.

Routes follow the registry: added accounts are walked from their first ledger, removed ones are dropped with the ledgers only they listed and those ledgers' rows; ledgers indexed under older rules or upto contracts are read again, and rows under an older registry version are re-attributed in place with the classifier's own attribution function.

Lag (the discovery source's head minus the ledger every route has walked), Lumeus request and error counts, candidate ledgers by status and failure metrics; health is degraded while behind and stopped after a failure.
Commits refresh the daily and per-account totals under a transaction-scoped advisory lock per network and epoch, so commits and removals that touch the same seller or day take turns.

threats.title: A compromised Explorer reaches the facilitator
threats.threat: The Explorer is public and parses attacker-chosen data; if it shared the facilitator's database or role, a compromise would read the settlement ledger and API keys or alter them.
threats.stellar: Every byte the indexer parses comes from public ledgers, where anyone can place transactions.
threats.preconditions: A code-execution or SQL bug in the Explorer.
threats.impact: Without protection: the facilitator's records and keys exposed through the public Explorer.

mitigations.text: A separate database with an owner, a writer and a reader role; the reader is SELECT-only with read-only transactions and a statement timeout; no Explorer role may connect to the facilitator's database.

Each process checks its role at startup and refuses superusers, role creators and any role that can reach the facilitator's database; the reader check also requires read-only, SELECT-only access with a timeout. The indexer holds no keys.

The reader's statement timeout is enforced by the client: each statement carries statement_timeout, and one still running after it is cancelled with pg_cancel_backend, so SET statement_timeout = 0 does not lift it. The writer cannot modify schema_migrations, and the indexer refuses a writer that can.

mitigations.text: The rebuild command writes canonical NDJSON sorted by position, aggregates and a manifest with the rules and registry versions, the ledger range and hashes, per-partition row hashes and file hashes; the same inputs give the same manifest hash.

A registry-scope report's manifest lists every ledger it read with its hash; `pnpm explorer:rebuild --ledgers-from manifest.json` reads those ledgers from the public data lake, with no discovery source, and writes the same manifest.

The report's network-wide block is a full-scope rebuild of a recent window by the same code; it prints its `pnpm explorer:rebuild --from --to` command (with `--anchor-horizon` when anchored) and its manifest is served at /api/v1/{network}/network-window/manifest, so anyone can rebuild that exact window and compare the hash.

threats.title: Indexing load starves the facilitator
threats.threat: Indexing every ledger (hundreds of gigabytes of downloads and tens of CPU-hours for pubnet history) runs on the host and database cluster the facilitator uses.
threats.stellar: Settlement latency matters: an x402 payment waits for the facilitator's answer.
threats.preconditions: An indexer running beside the facilitator.
threats.impact: Without protection: slower or failing settlements while history is indexed.

mitigations.text: The indexer never reads every ledger: discovery selects the ledgers that hold transactions of registry accounts and upto contracts, and only those are read, one object or one getLedgers page at a time. The full scan is a separate command run where its load does no harm.
Discovery and ledger reads share one limit of at most 8 requests in flight, as Lumeus asks for history walks; settings above it are refused.

Ledger reads hold at most EXPLORER_BYTES_IN_FLIGHT_MIB (64 MiB) of raw fetched bytes, size getLedgers pages to half of it and decode one ledger at a time, releasing it before the next, so a busy stretch of large ledgers cannot exhaust the indexer's memory; the bytes held are exported as rail402_explorer_ledger_bytes_in_flight.

The network-wide window is its own process, off unless EXPLORER_NETWORK_WINDOW_HOURS is set (at most 168 hours). Each run has a time budget, a download budget (required explicitly on pubnet) and a row budget, reads the data lake within a byte budget with one decoded ledger at a time and rows streamed to files it removes, and keeps the last published window when a budget stops it. It reads no Lumeus product and nothing of the facilitator.

threats.title: Alerts never arrive
threats.threat: The alerting stack runs on the host it watches; a host outage, a stopped Alertmanager or a broken notification channel means a sponsor drain or an outage goes unnoticed.
threats.stellar: A sponsor drain spends real XLM within the hour, and an unnoticed stale RPC stops settlement; both need a person within minutes.
threats.preconditions: A host, Prometheus or Alertmanager failure, or a misrouted channel.
threats.impact: Failures continue without anyone being told.

mitigations.text: Alertmanager sends an always-firing Watchdog alert every minute to an off-host dead-man's switch, which alerts by itself when the heartbeat stops.
Every alert in the catalog has a severity, an owner role and a runbook section; pages go to both on-call roles.

Prometheus scrapes each Explorer indexer, the Explorer web role and the hosted MCP endpoint by fixed target, so a stopped one stays a target; indexer down, indexing failures or chain breaks, lag, web down, MCP down and MCP upstream-budget refusals each raise a ticket.

A page silences only the tickets of its own cause on its own network (every channel busy covers channel lease timeouts, a stale RPC covers the failover away from it); every other alert is always sent, so an unrelated page never hides an independent failure.

The sponsor balance alert fires below each network's readiness floor and, on every network but testnet, below 100 XLM whatever the floor; pubnet refuses a floor below 1 XLM at startup, so a low, zero or missing floor never switches the page off.

threats.title: Monitoring components exposed, reached from the service, or used as a probe
threats.threat: A reachable Prometheus or Alertmanager leaks every series and lets anyone silence alerts; the blackbox exporter's /probe?target= becomes a request-forgery primitive into internal networks. The attacker who matters most is already inside: code execution in the facilitator, the process that holds the hot sponsor seed, could drain the sponsor and post a silence to Alertmanager's unauthenticated API so that no page fires, while the Watchdog heartbeat keeps the dead-man's switch green.
threats.stellar: The private metrics carry pubnet sponsor balances and budget figures, which tell an attacker when a drain would go unnoticed.
threats.preconditions: A published port or a route from the edge proxy to a monitoring service, or code execution in a container that shares a network with Alertmanager.
threats.impact: Information disclosure, silenced alerts, or requests to internal services.

mitigations.text: Monitoring services publish no port and sit only on internal networks; only Alertmanager has an outbound network, for notifications.

The networks are split by who may talk to whom: the facilitator replicas share only the scrape network with Prometheus and the blackbox exporter; Alertmanager sits on an alerting network with Prometheus alone, and node_exporter on its own network, so the service can reach neither.
Prometheus runs without its admin and lifecycle APIs, so whoever reaches it on the scrape network can read series but cannot delete them, reload rules or stop it.
The blackbox exporter allows only two modules without redirects, and Prometheus fixes every probe target.

threats.title: Database backups leak, are altered or cannot be restored
threats.threat: Off-host copies of the database carry key digests, settlement and usage records; a backup readable or writable by the wrong party leaks data or plants records on restore, and a backup that was never restored may not restore at all.
threats.stellar: The settlement ledger holds the recorded envelopes the reconciler needs to finish settlements after a loss; a database restored from a good point is safe because a payment already on chain can never settle again (its nonce is spent).
threats.preconditions: Access to the backup storage or its credentials, or a host loss.
threats.impact: Disclosure of usage and key digests, tampered records after a restore, or a database that cannot be recovered.

mitigations.text: Continuous WAL archiving with pgBackRest, encrypted with AES-256 before upload; the repository key and passphrase reach pgBackRest as a file secret, never as environment variables. The restore drill finds a marker row in the data files and nowhere in the repository.
Off-host copies are kept in two tiers that fit pgBackRest's rewrites and expiry: versioning with a host key that cannot delete versions, and object lock on the versions.
A restore drill restores to a point in time, compares every table's row count and checksum with the target, and checks that the runtime role still works.
Archiving failures, a growing archive backlog, a stale backup and a filling disk page the on-call.
With archiving on for 6 hours and no completed backup listed (none taken, or the repository unreadable), the stale-backup alert pages too.

threats.threat: A container escape from a co-located service, the host administrator path, or a DNS automation token that can edit every record lets an attacker read the pubnet seed or point the facilitator's host name at an impostor.
threats.stellar: A hot seed spends the sponsor's balance; an impostor facilitator can answer /supported with its own signers and refuse or misreport payments, but cannot move a payer's funds beyond what the payer signed.
threats.preconditions: Root on the host, or the DNS automation token.
threats.impact: Loss of the hot balance, or buyers and sellers talking to an impostor.

mitigations.text: The pubnet seed is a file secret readable only by the service user, and the cold key keeps sole control of the sponsor account, so a stolen hot seed cannot change signers.

threats.residual: Accepted while services share a host: root on the host can read the process memory, and the DNS token must be scoped and given an expiry by the operator; a dedicated host is the upgrade.

threats.title: Run funds stranded in accounts nobody can sign for, or that a stranger can sign for
threats.threat: A pubnet run funds smart accounts whose owner key is random and dropped, merges nothing, or stops on an exception or Ctrl-C before returning funds, and still reports the sweep as done; or a run account that whoever holds its key merged away is skipped as if it had never been created. Or a stranger makes itself the owner of a funded smart account (one whose owner is set by a call after it is created, which anyone can repeat), signs a transfer of its USDC to itself, and the sweep finds nothing to return.
threats.stellar: A contract account moves its USDC only with its owner's signature through __check_auth, and its own code decides whose signature that is; a constructor runs inside the transaction that creates the contract, so no other transaction can come first. A G account keeps its reserves until it is merged.
threats.preconditions: Any pubnet run with smart-account cases, an RPC error, a suite crash or an interrupt.
threats.impact: Without the controls: USDC and reserves lost on every run, or taken by a stranger, while the evidence claims they came back.

mitigations.text: Every run account and smart-account owner key is derived from the treasury seed and a role, and written to the run's owner-only registry (addresses and derivation paths, no secret) before it is funded; a contract account the run does not track, or whose owner it did not derive, is never funded.

The smart-account payer is a contract built in this repository whose constructor binds the derived owner key in the transaction that creates it; it exports no other function that writes state, so the key cannot be set first or changed afterwards.

Before the treasury sends USDC to a contract account, the run reads the account on chain and refuses it unless it runs the fixture account's code with the run's derived key as owner, or the OpenZeppelin smart account's code; a ledger it cannot read refuses too.

Sweep-back returns the USDC of every run account and smart account (authorised by the derived owner), merges the run accounts, then reads every balance again and fails the sweep-back case when anything is left, naming how much.
A run account the run saw on the network that is gone at the sweep (merged by whoever holds its key) fails the sweep; only an account the run never created is passed over.
Sweep-back runs once whatever happens: after the body, after an exception (rethrown afterwards) and on SIGINT or SIGTERM before the process exits.
After a crash, the registry is enough to return the funds of every account of the run.

threats.title: Third-party code a pubnet run starts reads the operator's secrets
threats.threat: The upstream e2e suite (third-party clients, servers and scripts) and the packages the live agent run installs with npm, with every dependency npm resolves for them, inherit the harness's environment: the treasury, sponsor and API key file paths, the run's ledger and its confirmation. npm runs the dependencies' install scripts, the installed SDK runs in the process that holds the treasury key, and the keys handed to that code (the suite's buyer, the agent's payer) keep receiving top-ups on later runs.
threats.stellar: A leaked Stellar seed moves the account's funds at once; nothing on chain can stop it.
threats.preconditions: A compromised or malicious commit in the suite checkout a mainnet run uses, or a compromised version of a package npm resolves for the live agent run.
threats.impact: Without the controls: the treasury drained, outside every cap.

mitigations.text: The suite runs with an allow-listed environment (toolchain variables minus anything that looks like a secret, token, key, confirmation or ledger) plus its own reviewed variables; a new suite variable is refused until it is added to the list.

The live agent run and pack-check install the packages with npm's lifecycle scripts off, so no dependency runs code while it installs, and with the same allow-listed environment; the code they install runs only in child processes that get that environment or less.

The live agent run never runs the installed packages in the process that holds the treasury: it starts an agent process with the allow-listed environment, which installs and runs them, and answers only its requests for the payer and for counting each payment.

On a host that allows it the agent process is launched in its own user, mount and PID namespaces (unshare): its /proc holds only its own processes, so it cannot read the treasury process's environment or memory, and the treasury secret file, the API key file and the runs directory are masked by an unreadable tmpfs. On pubnet, where the run holds a mainnet treasury, this is required: a run refuses to start before anything is spent on a host without it, unless the operator asserts, through a documented opt-out, that the agent runs under a separate OS user.

On pubnet the suite's buyer is derived from the treasury seed and the run id, fresh for each run and funded with 1 USDC, then swept and merged; the seller is a treasury-derived account, never the operator's sponsor.
On pubnet the live agent's payer is derived the same way, fresh for each run, so a seed the installed packages saw never controls a later run's payer.

threats.title: A pubnet run spends past its caps
threats.threat: The caps see estimates instead of the fees the network charges, miss contract deployments, count settlements once from a hand-made bound, apply to each harness process alone, and one confirmation authorises any number of reruns.
threats.stellar: Soroban fees come from simulation and include resource fees and rent; each settlement costs the facilitator's sponsor up to its fee ceiling.
threats.preconditions: A run with more cases, more settlements or higher fees than its estimates, or a rerun with the same confirmation.
threats.impact: Without the controls: real XLM and USDC spent beyond what the operator confirmed.

mitigations.text: Every transaction a harness submits passes one choke point: nothing is sent before the run's meter is attached, a fee the treasury pays is debited at its maximum before it is sent and lowered to the fee charged, and a fee source outside the run is refused.
Every /settle request to the target is debited at the facilitator's fee ceiling before it is sent, including those of the upstream suite through the harness's forwarder.
One ledger per evidence run, shared by every harness process under a lock, caps the run's net XLM and net USDC loss; its id includes a fresh nonce, it is claimed once and closed at the end.
Caps and fee ceilings are required on pubnet and refused when malformed or zero.

threats.title: A pubnet run pays through the wrong contract or without access
threats.threat: Pubnet upto clients ignore the configured contract, a contract setting points at code other than the published one, or a run against a keyed facilitator funds its accounts and then has every request refused.
threats.stellar: An upto payer authorises the settlement contract it is given; another contract with the same interface would receive the authorisation.
threats.preconditions: A pubnet run with upto cases or against a facilitator that requires keys.
threats.impact: Without the controls: authorisations signed for unverified code, or funds spent on a run that cannot pass.

mitigations.text: The upto contract and its WASM hash are taken together, checked against the published pubnet deployment record when it exists, and the contract's instance is read on chain before anything is spent; every pubnet harness passes it to its upto clients.
Before anything is spent, an empty /verify shows whether the facilitator serves the run; a missing or refused key stops it, and the key is then sent with every facilitator request.

threats.title: A seller names its own settlement authority for a pubnet upto payment
threats.threat: A seller puts a key it controls in an upto option's extra.facilitatorAddress, so it can settle the full cap whatever the call used, or switches the authority between the confirmation and the signature.
threats.stellar: An upto authorization lets the named settlement authority move up to the cap through the pinned upto contract; whoever holds that authority decides how much of the cap is settled.
threats.preconditions: A pubnet buyer with upto enabled (an explicit pinned upto contract).
threats.impact: The full cap is charged for a call that used less, within the caps the user approved.

mitigations.text: On pubnet a buyer that can sign upto pins the authorities it accepts: the policy's uptoFacilitators (RAIL402_UPTO_FACILITATORS), or else the facilitatorAddress values its facilitator advertises for upto on pubnet in /supported, read once when the buyer is created; without either it refuses to open (payment_policy_invalid). Any other authority is refused before signing.
The authority is shown in the MCP and CLI prompts and bound in the sealed MCP intent, so a different authority on the retry is asked about again.

threats.title: The sponsor seed handled on a networked machine during setup
threats.threat: The one-time signer setup is signed with the hot seed; doing that on a networked workstation with the full dependency tree lets a compromised dependency capture the seed before the account has its cold signer.
threats.stellar: Until the setup applies, the seed is the account's only signer and meets every threshold, so whoever holds it can take the account over.
threats.preconditions: A compromised development dependency or workstation at setup time.
threats.impact: The new sponsor account taken over before the cold signer exists.

mitigations.text: The setup is built unsigned on the networked machine (optionally with the sequence given, without any network) and signed on the offline machine by the zero-dependency key tool, which refuses a key tagged for another network and an envelope that is already signed; only the signed XDR crosses back.
The unsigned setup and its review come from the ceremony tool without the seed.

threats.title: Discovery leaves out or invents candidate ledgers
threats.threat: The discovery source, or someone between it and the indexer, leaves ledgers out of an account's or contract's activity, lists ledgers that hold nothing, or answers for another route, window or network.
threats.stellar: Activity records are decoded data a service computes from ledgers; nothing on chain commits to them. The ledgers themselves are bound by their hashes.
threats.preconditions: A faulty or dishonest discovery source, or control of the connection to it.
threats.impact: Without protection: invented settlements, settlements silently missing from pages and totals, or unbounded reads (billed on mainnet) of ledgers a source lists.

mitigations.text: Discovery only selects ledgers: every row comes from a ledger read in full, verified against its own hashes (and anchors where configured) and classified by the unchanged rules, so discovery cannot create a settlement that is not on chain. A listed ledger that holds no registry transaction adds only that ledger's own real rows (unattributed look-alikes, failed attempts, exclusion counts); the manifest lists it and the report counts such ledgers (ledgersWithoutAttributedRow).

Activity pages are checked: the first page pins the read view and later pages must keep it, every record must lie inside the requested window, the page must be for the indexer's network, and next links must stay on the same origin and route.

The report states its scope and lists every ledger read; the full-scan audit command reads every ledger of the range from the public data lake, and its attributed rows must equal the report's, which shows an omission.

Each upto contract whose settlements emit an event has its own contract route; a concluded beta contract, which emits no event and moves no funds itself (its contract activity is empty), is found through topic search for the token approve events that name it as the spender, which each of its settlements carries in the same transaction.

A route adds at most EXPLORER_MAX_CANDIDATES_PER_ROUND new candidate ledgers per round and continues next round, counted in rail402_explorer_candidates_capped_total; candidates with no attributed row are counted in rail402_explorer_candidates_unattributed_total.

The report counts only rows of the ledgers its manifest lists, whatever else the tables hold, and the move to registry scope removes every row, total and report of the earlier full scan; a stored report of another scope or manifest version is never served.

threats.title: The Lumeus key leaks or reaches another host
threats.threat: The Lumeus server key is set inline in the environment, logged, sent to a host that is not Lumeus (a configured URL, a next link, a redirect), or a testnet key is used against mainnet hosts or the reverse.
threats.stellar: Lumeus keys are per network: lum_test_ for testnet, lum_live_ for mainnet; one key covers Activity and RPC.
threats.preconditions: A misconfiguration, a hostile next link or redirect, or access to logs or the process environment.
threats.impact: Without protection: a stolen key spends the organisation's Lumeus credits.

mitigations.text: The key is read only from a file (EXPLORER_LUMEUS_KEY_FILE, EXPLORER_<NETWORK>_LUMEUS_KEY_FILE); an inline key is refused, and no error repeats it.
The key is sent only to the network's own Lumeus host for that product: Activity and RPC URLs are checked against an allow-list, and a key's prefix must match the network.

RPC clients (the ledger source and the web live lookup) attach the key only for the Lumeus RPC host of its network and refuse any other pairing; next links to another origin and redirects are refused.
